Last term, I lost more study hours to “quick chai?” than to anything else. I'm Elizabeth. I'd be in the library with my stats notes, and my friend Irawati would message: “Canteen? Ten minutes.” I'd go. Ten minutes became ninety. Every time.
This term, before exams started, I wrote a plan on the first page of my notebook: “If Irawati asks me out between 2 and 6, I'll say: ‘Later! Six o'clock at the canteen?’ and go back to my page.”
It felt silly. But the first time her message came, I didn't have to decide anything. I just typed the line.
She sent a thumbs up. At six, we had chai, and I actually enjoyed it, because I wasn't guilty.
I planned for the exact thing that always got me. That was the difference.

qa.q: What line did Elizabeth plan to send when Irawati asked?
qa.a: “Later! Six o'clock at the canteen?”

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel at chai at six this term?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt relaxed and free of guilt, enjoying the break because the study hours had been protected.

qa.q: Why did planning for the specific obstacle work?
qa.a: Elizabeth knew exactly what to do when the invitation came, so there was no in-the-moment decision to lose.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about the new “later”?
qa.a: Irawati seems fine with it, sending a thumbs up and still getting time with her friend at six.

Learning-support tutor's note, first-year cohort, week 8.
Pranav came to me in week 3, frustrated. He had planned four-hour library blocks and kept losing them. The main thing that broke them: his friend Sudha, who finishes classes early, messaging him to come for a walk or snacks.
He didn't want to say no to her, and he didn't want to lose the hours.
We wrote one line together: “If Sudha invites me out between 2 and 6, then I'll say ‘Later, six o'clock?’ and stay.” He saved it as a reply template on his phone.
I observed him in the library last Tuesday. His phone lit up; he read it, smiled, tapped once and went back to his notes. At six I saw them leave together.
He reports finishing three of four planned blocks this week, up from one.
Next step: we will add a similar plan for his other obstacle, the evening hostel cricket.

On 1 January I wrote “Get healthier” in big letters on my whiteboard. I'm Vaibhav, twenty-four, and I really meant it.
I didn't write anything else. No time, no plan. I just thought, I'll eat better and move more.
In the first week I had fruit for breakfast and took the stairs twice. Then there was a deadline at work, then my cousin's wedding, then a cold. Each time I thought I'd get back to it. I never picked a day.
By February, my breakfast was two samosas from the stall under the office again. I noticed the whiteboard one evening, still saying “Get healthier,” and felt a mix of guilt and annoyance.
My colleague Ishita, who cycles every morning at 6:30 without fail, once told me, “I don't decide. It's just what happens after my alarm.”
That's what I was missing. A “when.”

Imran, you keep saying you'll start stretching and never do. Let me, your old boss Ramesh, tell you how I finally managed it at twenty-four.
I had a desk job in Chennai and a back like a plank. Every evening I promised myself I'd stretch “later.” Later never came. I'd think about it at night and feel lazy.
Then a colleague, an older lady named Thangam, told me, “Don't look for time. Tie it to something you already do.”
So I tied it to brushing my teeth. Toothbrush back in the cup, and I'd do five stretches right there at the sink. My wife thought I'd gone mad.
The first few days I had to remind myself. After two weeks, my hands put down the brush and my body just bent. I didn't have to think.
Thirty years later, I still do it every morning.

qa.a: Ramesh felt lazy and guilty, promising “later” every evening and never doing it.

qa.a: When Ramesh tied the stretches to brushing teeth; after two weeks the stretches happened without thinking.

qa.a: She probably felt amused and puzzled at first, thinking Ramesh had gone mad.

The college in Hoshangabad had one printer, and it closed at 10 a.m. Mridul's project report was due at 10:30.
At 9 p.m. the night before, he hadn't started. He grinned at his friend Neelam across the hostel verandah. “Watch me. Pressure is when I shine.”
And for a while he did. His fingers flew. He felt alive, buzzing, almost happy.
By 2 a.m. the power went off. He wrote by candle. By 5, his head was pounding.
At 9:45 he ran to the printer with a pen drive. The report had two pages in the wrong order and no references.
Neelam, who had finished hers last week, handed him a glass of water. “Did you shine?”
Mridul, pale and sweating, managed a laugh. “For about three hours.”

Rafael had always said he wrote best at 3 a.m. At his university in Lisbon, it was a bit of a legend. His flatmate Jin had seen it many times: nothing for two weeks, then a wild all-nighter, loud music, energy drinks, and a paper finished at dawn.
This semester Rafael had three papers due in the same week. He left all three.
The first all-nighter went fine. He felt thrilled, like a hero in a film. The second, his hands shook. The third, he fell asleep at the desk at 4 a.m. and woke at 8, with half a page done.
Jin found him staring at his screen, grey-faced. “You okay?”
“I don't think the panic works when there are three,” Rafael said.
He got an extension on the third paper, but lost marks. He also caught a cold that lasted two weeks.

Pranav, you're asking whether to apply for the design job, the MA, or the start-up internship, and you've been “thinking” for four months. Let me, your Jeevan Tata, tell you about 1978.
I was twenty-two, just graduated from Mangalore. I had three choices: a bank job, a teaching post, and a scholarship to study geology.

The bank post filled. The scholarship deadline passed. Only the teaching job was still open, so I took it.
It turned out fine, mind you. I liked teaching. But I didn't choose it. It chose me, because I waited.

At 11:50 it came back. The Pune form needed an essay he hadn't written. The corporate one had closed at 11:30.

Seema had finished her engineering degree in May. It was now October. On her laptop was a spreadsheet: twelve job openings, four master's programmes, two gap-year volunteering posts. Columns for salary, city, “regret risk.”

Her friend Rukmini visited with jalebis. “Still the spreadsheet?”

“And if you don't choose?”
“Then I'm keeping all doors open.”

Seema stared at the red cells. For the first time, she felt the fear shift from making the wrong choice to making none at all.

In the second-year hostel in Jaipur, Sumit had heard Asif say it a dozen times: “Tomorrow I'll start the lab report. Properly.”
Every tomorrow, Asif ended up playing cricket or scrolling. And every night, he looked more miserable. Last night he'd said, “I'm useless, bhai,” and turned to face the wall.

My friend Zainab has been “starting tomorrow” on her dissertation proposal for three weeks. I'm Jyoti; we share a room in the hostel.
Every night she'd say, “Tomorrow, first thing.” Every next night she'd be quieter, more tired, scrolling in the dark. On Thursday she said, “I'm such a failure,” and I felt something twist in my chest. She's not. She's the smartest person I know.
So on Friday morning I put my laptop next to hers and said, “Twenty minutes. I'll work on my stuff, you just write the title and three possible research questions. Bad ones are fine.”
She laughed a little. She wrote the title. Then the three questions. Then she added a fourth.
When the timer rang, she didn't stop.
That night she didn't say “tomorrow.” She said, “I'll do the literature bit after breakfast.” That sounded different.
